messages.author: 0ee8ae7c0d185529
messages.subject: "Standard" Chi-Square for WLSMV
parts:
Hi all,

I am running an analysis that compares a number of approaches to handling non-normality.  I am finding that the WLSMV chi-square under the "Standard" column is very much lower than the robust column and also very much lower than the same column for MLR.  For example, the standard chi-square for MLR is 770.994 compared to 168.287.  Similarly, for WLS the standard chi-square is 690.2 compared to 168.287 for the WLSMV standard chi-square.  I'm not sure I have seen such large differences.  Any thoughts?

Thanks!

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: "Standard" Chi-Square for WLSMV
parts: standard chi-square for MLR is 770.994 compared to 168.287.  Similarly, for WLS the standard chi-square is 690.2 compared to 168.287 for the WLSMV standard chi-square.  I'm not sure I have seen such large differences.  Any thoughts?

For MLR (Huber-White / sandwich-style scaling factor) , the discrepancy (quantified by the scaling factor) depends on the levels of the kurtosis because the standard chi-squared is scaled using fourth-order moments.  A recent pub describes how to derive expected moments (1-4) for normal data discretized by given thresholds:  https://doi.org/10.1080/10705511.2021.1988609
I expect there should be an analytical solution to derive the scaling factor, too.  But I expect it is informative enough to simply check the univariate kurtosis of your descriptives, e.g., using psych::describe() 

For DWLS with a scaled and shifted statistic, I think the scale and shift parameters depend on the amount of uncertainty when estimating the thresholds and polychoric correlations.  Although not adjusted for nonnormality per se, they should be indirectly dependent on the nonnormality of the discrete observations.  For example, I would expect that highly skewed discrete observations must have fewer observations in extreme categories, which makes those thresholds less certain, and thus polychorics involving such variables less certain.  Thus, I expect highly skewed discrete observations to also have more extreme scale/shift parameters.
